articles.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
articles.summary: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.   Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research […]
articles.content:
NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA/Jonathan North

NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.

Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.

“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”

Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall, a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.

As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base, and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.

Key design decisions

The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.

One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.

Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft. Credit: NASA/David Lam

NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its nuclear power module, and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.

In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s Power and Propulsion Element by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.

NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.

Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.

Updated mission profile

Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.

After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.

NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA

After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space.

“By refining the design and advancing this architecture, we’re not just building a spacecraft, we’re establishing the foundation for a new era of reliable, efficient transport beyond Earth orbit,” Sinacore said. “What we learn from SR-1 Freedom will shape the future of exploration for decades to come.”

With key design decisions advancing and teams across NASA, DOE, and industry working together, SR-1 Freedom is moving toward its 2028 launch goal. The mission will demonstrate new capabilities for nuclear-powered transportation and help establish the foundation for future exploration beyond Earth.

To learn more about NASA’s efforts in nuclear power in space, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/space-nuclear

articles.personality_title: NASA finalizes design for first nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is preparing a new spacecraft called Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, designed to use nuclear power to travel beyond Earth’s orbit. This spacecraft will test nuclear electric propulsion, a powerful way to move in space, helping future missions go farther and last longer.

**What happened** – In October 2023, experts from NASA, the U.S. Department of Energy, and industry partners met to review and lock in key parts of SR-1’s design. The spacecraft is planned to launch in 2028 and will carry a capsule named SkyFall with three helicopters to Mars. The team decided to use a shorter arm (boom) to hold the nuclear reactor, making the spacecraft lighter and simpler. They also improved safety shields so the reactor can be closer to other parts of the spacecraft. A new heat system to keep the reactor cool is being developed by Johns Hopkins University, with help from a commercial partner.

**Impact** – This mission is the first time a nuclear reactor will power a spacecraft traveling beyond Earth orbit. Nuclear power can provide more energy than solar panels, especially far from the Sun or in places with little sunlight. This means longer missions and more powerful tools on spacecraft and future Moon bases. The SR-1 mission will help NASA learn how to use nuclear power safely and effectively in space, opening new possibilities for exploring Mars and beyond.

**What’s next step** – After launch, the spacecraft will gradually turn on its nuclear reactor and collect data to show how well it works. It will deliver the SkyFall capsule to Mars, then restart the reactor to continue testing. Meanwhile, the team will keep refining the design, focusing on reducing risks and making the spacecraft ready on time for the 2028 launch.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s SR-1 Freedom will be the first nuclear-powered spacecraft beyond Earth orbit, testing new technology to enable deeper, longer space missions starting with Mars in 2028.

articles.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
articles.summary: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory […]
articles.content:
Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project!

Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When gravitational wave detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.

The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar Impact Flash! project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

"Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background."

The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”

To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/ or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!

articles.title: The mystery of sub-Neptunes – the planets we thought shouldn’t exist
articles.summary: Sub-Neptunes are the most abundant exoplanets, but are unlike anything in our solar system. We are finally gaining tantalising clues about what they are and how they came to be
articles.content:
Sub-Neptunes are the most abundant exoplanets, but are unlike anything in our solar system. We are finally gaining tantalising clues about what they are and how they came to be

Christian Gralingen

For almost a decade, the Kepler Space Telescope trailed Earth’s orbit, watching out for flickers in the light of distant stars. In 2011, two years after its launch, the NASA mission found what it was looking for: the signature of a roughly Earth-sized planet dimming out a tiny sliver of light as it transited across the face of its star.

The identification of Kepler-10b, a planet almost 1.5 times the size of Earth that orbits a star around 600 light years away, was the first time we had spotted a rocky exoplanet – a world beyond our solar system. Since then, our rapidly expanding exoplanet catalogue has revealed plenty of surprises, but one above all: most planets in our galaxy aren’t like Earth. In fact, they are like nothing in our solar system at all.

Out of the now 6451 confirmed exoplanets, by far the most common type are the “sub-Neptunes”, planets between Earth and Neptune in size that old theories of planet formation based on our solar system didn’t predict. And there are lots of them – over 3000 at the last count. “You know how evolution, like, really likes making crabs? Planet formation seems to really like making sub-Neptunes,” says astrophysicist Matthew Nixon at Arizona State University.

Advertisement

But there is no sub-Neptune in our solar system, and that leaves researchers with a puzzle: what exactly are these mysterious planets? Now, aided by NASA’s orbiting high-tech thermal camera, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), they are coming into sharper focus. New discoveries are answering some questions, but raising many more about what sub-Neptunes look like, how they form – and whether they might even host life.

Exoplanetary science is still young. Astronomers spotted the first planet beyond our solar system, a gas giant circling a pulsar, in 1992. In 1995 came the first exoplanet around a sun-like star, a giant, close-orbiting “hot Jupiter” called 51 Pegasi b. But the hunt didn’t hit its high season until Kepler launched in 2009. It flew with just one instrument: a photometer that could precisely measure stars’ brightness and catch the telltale flickers of passing planets. By the time the mission ran out of fuel in 2018, it had discovered over half of all exoplanets we know today.

Back in those early days, our ideas of how planets formed were guided by a sample of one: our solar system. It is widely agreed that our sun formed from the gravitational collapse of the solar nebula, a giant, spinning cloud of hydrogen and helium gas, plus a sprinkling of heavier elements. Once the young sun ignited, a disc of material continued circling it that would give rise to the planets.

Neptune is one of two ice giant planets in the outer reaches of our solar system NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI), Naomi Rowe-Gurney (NASA-GSFC)

Looking at our solar system, scientists broadly concluded that what planets look like came down to where they formed within this nebular Frisbee. Closer to the sun, it is too hot for anything but rock and metals to solidify and clump together, meaning less material to sweep up into planets. So, the planets of the inner solar system – Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars – ended up small and rocky. Meanwhile, in longer orbits beyond the “snow line”, where compounds such as water, ammonia and methane freeze out and form ices, baby planetary cores could get bigger. These bigger cores had the gravitational heft to gobble up hydrogen and helium gas from the solar nebula. They formed the outer solar system’s two gas giants, Jupiter and Saturn, and its more distant “ice giants”, Uranus and Neptune.

Earth is the solar system’s largest rocky planet; Neptune, at around four times Earth’s diameter, is its smallest giant planet. The gap in size between the two seemed natural. Given how we thought planets form, worlds much bigger than Earth should be incredibly rare within the snow line. That, it turns out, isn’t true.

Exoplanet astronomers have found everything from alien gas titans that would dwarf Jupiter to planetary pebbles comparable to Mercury. But among confirmed exoplanets with a known radius, about half are sub-Neptunes, many of them hewing in warm orbits very close to their stars. “They’re really the ultimate mystery,” says exoplanet astronomer Eliza Kempton at the University of Chicago.

Kempton has been studying sub-Neptunes since before they were called sub-Neptunes. In 2010, even before Kepler found that first Earth-sized planet, she and her colleagues used the ground-based Very Large Telescope facility in Chile to observe the hazy atmosphere of a planet called GJ 1214 b some 48 light years away from Earth. With a radius 2.7 times that of Earth, but orbiting far closer to its star than Mercury does to the sun, that planet is now something of a poster child for the sub-Neptunes. But back then, it was a “super-Earth”.

“We just called everything a super-Earth,” says Kempton. “This was before we even knew that small planets bifurcate into, like, the ‘smaller’ class and the ‘bigger’ class.” That divide refers to a striking discovery made in 2017 that deepened the mystery of sub-Neptunes further still. When astronomers used Kepler data to chart the number of exoplanets of different sizes, it revealed two bumps. One was centred on planets with radii about 1.4 times Earth’s, and another on those of about 2.4 Earth radii. In between, there was a gap with relatively few planets. The sub-Neptunes appeared to be not just one population of planets, but two.

The discovery of this “radius valley” lent support to an idea that harsh radiation emitted from young stars, plus leftover heat from planet formation, blasts away the baby blankets of hydrogen and helium gas enveloping smaller planets. That leaves bare, rocky worlds that form the super-Earth peak. Bigger planets with more gravity, meanwhile, hold onto at least some hydrogen and helium. They end up as puffier, gas-cloaked worlds in the sub-Neptune peak.

In this picture, terrestrial planets like Earth might be the naked cores of erstwhile sub-Neptunes. “If you’re ultimately interested in more Earth-like worlds, sub-Neptunes represent a kind of arrested stage of development. These are the things that stop short of becoming something like Earth,” says planetary scientist Raymond Pierrehumbert at the University of Oxford. “I think of them almost like fossilised atmospheres.”



Unlike the ice giants of our solar system, sub-Neptunes close to their stars might form pretty dry – as “gas dwarfs” with no ice, just a rocky interior and a thick gas envelope made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. But there are other possibilities. The discovery of hot Jupiters – gas giant planets in close orbits where they couldn’t possibly have formed – helped scientists realise that planets can migrate, something we now know probably happened in our solar system, too. Sub-Neptunes could be ice worlds that form beyond their planetary system’s snow line and wander inwards. In some simulations, this migration produces a radius valley: one that divides small, rocky planets from big, watery ones.



Since JWST’s launch in 2021, astronomers have been able to start differentiating between such scenarios. Its great infrared eye sees in wavelengths of light at which molecules such as water, ammonia, carbon dioxide and methane leave distinctive fingerprints on starlight passing through exoplanets’ upper atmospheres.

In at least one case, that of the hot sub-Neptune TOI-421 b, which orbits its sun-like star far closer than Mercury does our sun, JWST observations largely match what you would expect for a gas dwarf. But observations are revealing that sub-Neptunes are a diverse group (see “Five ways to make a sub-Neptune”, below). If some of them are worlds with abundant water, it would be a big deal for the search for life. “Where you can find water, you can find habitable conditions,” says astrophysicist Caroline Piaulet-Ghorayeb also at the University of Chicago. Finding sub-Neptune water worlds “would kind of change our thinking about habitability”, she says. Earth-sized planets are very hard to observe in detail with JWST, so bigger water worlds could be our best immediate hope for finding signs of life on an exoplanet.

The mere presence of water doesn’t make a habitable planet. Sub-Neptunes could be balls of exotic, high-pressure ice and “supercritical” fluids that are neither liquid nor gas – mini ice giants, not ocean worlds. And because hydrogen is a strong greenhouse gas, sub-Neptunes with hydrogen atmospheres can end up as boiling “steam worlds” with atmospheres rich in water vapour. JWST observations suggest that a watery sub-Neptune called GJ 9827 d is such a planet.

However, in the lead-up to JWST’s launch, astrophysicist Nikku Madhusudhan at the University of Cambridge and his colleagues showed that water worlds with thin hydrogen atmospheres could have liquid water on their surfaces (too thick an atmosphere, and the water boils). Madhusudhan later dubbed these planets “Hycean” worlds, a portmanteau of “hydrogen” and “ocean”. JWST observations have hinted that a sub-Neptune called K2-18 b orbiting a star some 125 light years from Earth might belong to this group. It sits in its star’s habitable zone, where it is theoretically cool enough for surface liquid water.

The James Webb Space Telescope has revolutionised the study of exoplanet atmospheres NASA/MSFC/David Higginbotham

This plot thickened in 2023, when Madhusudhan’s team spotted what it interpreted as tentative evidence for dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in K2-18 b’s atmosphere. On Earth, DMS is made only by life – primarily plankton in the ocean. The team doubled down after follow-up JWST observations, but the result remains fiercely disputed. Nixon objects that the data isn’t enough to uniquely identify a molecule as complex as DMS. “A lot of other molecules, if you were to test them, you would also get a comparable result,” he says. Madhusudhan stands by the detection. He argues that researchers have historically accepted detections of more mundane gases like CO2 based on comparable evidence.

If there is DMS on K2-18 b, it is possible that an unknown chemical process might produce it, rather than alien microbes. Madhusudhan says he would “absolutely” be happy either way. “The discovery of a new chemical process in a planetary atmosphere? I mean, that’s a huge deal,” he says. “To me, that is as good as finding life.”

But even the identification of K2-18 b as a Hycean world is disputed. What scientists see in sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres depends in large part on what happens out of view, deep in the planets’ hot, high-pressure interiors. The mix of molecules JWST has spotted in K2-18 b’s atmosphere matches a planet with water oceans – but might also fit a gaseous mini-Neptune without a real surface, or a gas dwarf with a magma ocean simmering below its hydrogen envelope.

Earth once had a magma ocean, too. Rocky worlds go through an initial molten phase with a global magma ocean before they cool down and solidify. Some sub-Neptunes might trap enough primordial heat below blankets of gas and icy material that their magma oceans never freeze – with significant consequences. “Magma oceans are a chemical factory,” says Pierrehumbert. “Chemicals can get in there and react and do all sorts of stuff.” One reason to think K2-18 b is a watery world is the lack of ammonia in its atmosphere: ammonia dissolves in water. But it also dissolves in liquid rock. So ultimately, researchers need to learn more about K2-18 b’s atmosphere to pin down its composition.

Magma oceans do more than conceal compounds such as ammonia – they “fundamentally change the composition of the atmosphere”, says Kempton. Reactions between hydrogen and magma could even produce abundant water on planets that were born dry, without any water, she adds. This process might have produced some of Earth’s water back when it had a magma ocean.

Magma isn’t the only thing that might be smouldering deep within sub-Neptunes. A study led by Kempton’s University of Chicago colleague Jeehyun Yang recently found that sub-Neptunes could be a bit like combustion engines, burning carbon-rich compounds to produce soot. A layer of these planets might be, rather literally, on fire, says Yang. Clouds of black soot belched up from below would block out some molecular signals, perhaps explaining a pattern of muted molecular fingerprints in JWST data from several sub-Neptunes.

Some worlds might make soot; others might actually be made of it. Just as there is a snow line beyond which water is solid, there is a “soot line” around young stars where organic carbon molecules can start to form grains of black, tarry material. Sub-Neptunes are reviving an old idea that this could create “soot worlds”, says planetary scientist Zifan Lin at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri. Lin and his colleague Sara Seager at the University of Toronto recently showed that soot worlds with cores of rock and metal, overlain by layers of diamond and graphite and with hydrogen-rich atmospheres, could match JWST observations of three sub-Neptunes, including K2-18 b.

So, gas dwarfs, water worlds, soot planets – what’s the answer? The boundaries might be fuzzier than they sound. Recent work by Piaulet-Ghorayeb and her colleagues has shown that some sub-Neptunes that appear dry could hide water deep in their interiors, where it is invisible to telescopes. And there could be sooty water worlds, sooty gas dwarfs and everything in between.

One lesson sub-Neptunes have already taught scientists is that planetary evolution, not just formation, determines what worlds are made of. Losing an atmosphere or reacting one with a magma ocean, say, shapes a planet just as profoundly as forming beyond or within the snow line. Nixon says he is working on finding ways to distinguish between water worlds that wandered inwards and sub-Neptunes that formed dry and later made their own water. To this end, he is observing a hot sub-Neptune called HD 86226 that is virtually guaranteed to have a magma ocean, eliminating some guesswork.

Ideally, scientists would eventually like to understand whether sub-Neptunes are all basically variations on the same planetary theme, or are many sub-groups with different histories. Observations so far have pinpointed only a few molecules in a handful of sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres. Surveys of more sub-Neptunes are under way, and these could help pick out different groups if they exist.

The more we learn about sub-Neptunes, the more they surprise us, making them one of the most exciting active frontiers in exoplanetary science. We still don’t know why our solar system lacks one of these abundant worlds, but they are the closest thing to a world like Earth that we can observe easily at present. Through them, we learn not only about the broader universe, but also about the forces that sculpt worlds like our own. “The sub-Neptunes give us that next stepping stone,” says Kempton. “We’re kind of marching our way towards the study of Earth-like worlds in the future.”

articles.personality_title: New insights into sub-Neptune planets reveal surprising diversity and clues about their origins
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have discovered thousands of planets outside our solar system, called exoplanets. Among them, sub-Neptunes—planets larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune—are the most common. However, these planets do not exist in our solar system, making them a mystery.

**What happened** – Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in 2021, astronomers have started to study the atmospheres of sub-Neptunes in detail. This telescope can detect gases like water vapor and methane by analyzing the light from stars that passes through these planets’ atmospheres. Recent observations have revealed that sub-Neptunes are a varied group, including dry gas-covered planets, water-rich worlds, and even planets with thick soot clouds.

**Impact** – These findings are important because they challenge old ideas about how planets form and evolve. Scientists now understand that sub-Neptunes can have very different compositions and histories, including some that might hold liquid water. This expands the types of planets that could potentially support life and helps us learn more about how planets like Earth might develop.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to study more sub-Neptunes to better understand their differences and origins. They want to find out if these planets form in similar ways or if there are many types with unique stories. Future observations will also help clarify if some sub-Neptunes could be habitable or even show signs of life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New observations with the James Webb Space Telescope are revealing that sub-Neptune planets come in many forms, helping scientists solve the mystery of these common but previously unknown worlds and opening new paths to study planets beyond our solar system.

articles.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
articles.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.
articles.content:
The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system. Images captured between September 16 and 24, 2026, revealed a previously unknown comet, the first discovered by the mission.

The achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets. The speed with which researchers identified and confirmed the discovery demonstrates that Euclid can detect new comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun. This capability could eventually help identify a target for ESA's upcoming Comet Interceptor mission.

A Mysterious Streak Reveals a New Comet

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium. Pöntinen developed specialized software to detect and track small solar system objects appearing in the telescope's images.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images -- the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas."

The object appeared in a region of the sky known as the 'Euclid Deep Field North'. Over several days, the telescope captured it in five separate fields of view, taking between two and four exposures of each field for a total of 16 exposures.

After searching catalogs of known asteroids and comets without finding a match, Pöntinen submitted the observations to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a potential new comet. The report enabled astronomers using telescopes on Earth to carry out additional observations. On October 8, the MPC officially confirmed the discovery. The comet has been designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

A Comet on an Extraordinary Orbit

The newly discovered comet is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth. That distance is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point somewhere between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

However, the comet is traveling well outside the relatively flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun. It is currently positioned almost directly above the Sun, following a sweeping path over the solar system that will take thousands of years to complete.

The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) serves as the central international hub for observations of asteroids and comets. It gathers data from observers around the world to verify discoveries, determine orbital paths, and assign official designations. As additional observations become available, astronomers will be able to calculate the orbital period of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) more precisely.

Why Euclid Rarely Discovers New Comets

Although Euclid has spotted comets before, all of them had already been discovered. Several aspects of the telescope's design and observing strategy make finding previously unknown objects within our solar system especially difficult.

Euclid intentionally avoids the region of the sky surrounding the plane of the solar system, where large numbers of asteroids and comets can be found. Dust concentrated in this region produces unwanted light that could interfere with the telescope's sensitive observations of the distant universe.

The spacecraft also follows a 'step-and-stare' observing strategy, typically imaging each section of the sky only once. This means researchers cannot readily direct Euclid back toward a newly detected comet to gather more information about it.

Identifying objects within our solar system is nevertheless an important part of Euclid's scientific work. Researchers must account for everything appearing in its images so that unrelated features, including comet trails and unwanted light, can be removed without compromising the accuracy of its galaxy measurements.

"Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet's orbit and Euclid's scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images," says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, and part of the discovery team.

Preparing for a Future Comet Encounter

Euclid's unexpected discovery also provides valuable experience for scientists working on ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission. Although the newly identified comet is not an appropriate destination for the spacecraft, the successful detection and rapid notification process demonstrates how the two missions could work together to identify potential targets.

"While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on," adds Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

Ancient Remnants of the Solar System

Comets are ancient bodies composed of ice and dust that remain from the formation of our solar system approximately 4.6 billion years ago. Most originate in the distant Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, regions located beyond the orbits of the outer planets (interstellar comets come from other solar systems).

As a comet approaches the Sun, increasing temperatures cause its ice to turn directly into gas. Escaping gas and dust form a glowing, fuzzy cloud known as a 'coma,' as well as an extended tail.

Because comets native to our solar system have remained relatively unchanged since their formation, they preserve valuable evidence of the materials and environmental conditions that existed when the planets were taking shape. Studying these ancient objects may also help scientists understand the origins of Earth's water and the chemical building blocks of life.

Euclid's Hunt for Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The primary goal of the Euclid mission is to uncover how dark matter and dark energy influence the visible universe. During its six-year survey, the space telescope will examine the shapes and movements of billions of galaxies at distances reaching up to 10 billion light-years.

The comet discovery was reported on behalf of the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium by M. Pöntinen, A. A. Nucita, A. Franco, M. Granvik, B. Altieri, S. Kruk, B. Y. Irureta-Goyena and B. Carry.

articles.personality_title: ESA’s Euclid telescope discovers a new comet in our solar system
articles.personality_presentation:

A student named Mikko Pöntinen used special software to find the comet’s moving streak in the telescope’s images. After checking with astronomers worldwide, the comet was officially confirmed and named C/2026 S1 (Euclid).
